newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr holed by rate risk, plumbs 17-mth low.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr holed by rate risk, plumbs 17-mth low.

text.p: The Australian dollar was listing at 17-month lows at the midsession with support so full of holes bulls had to bail furiously just to stay afloat at US$0.7440.
Most of the market was either too busy trying to second guess the Reserve Bank to lend a hand or just disinclined having been badly caught out by three of the bank's last four easings.

Every dealer had a pet theory on what the RBA would do and when it would do it. These ranged from a full 50 basis point cut Wednesday morning to a delay until Thursday or late July or even the following board meeting in August; a 0.25 point easing now and another later; or simply no cut at all.
That last view began to gain a little popularity amongst forex dealers last week, but the majority of economists favour a cut either this month or next.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the local currency was down at US$0.7445/50 having been holed by U.S. investment bank selling late Friday after it closed here at US$0.7484/89.

On the crosses it eased to 85.10/20 yen from 85.42/47 with the losses tempered by a firm performance from US$/yen. But it looked vulnerable against the Canadian dollar and sterling, two currencies benefiting from rising domestic interest rates.
In trade weighted terms it slid to 56.7 from 56.9.
That a fifth official cut is being contemplated at all reflects a seachange in perceptions about the strength of both the economy and the RBA's commitment to cutting unemployment.
Just over a month ago most analysts had doubted even a fourth cut was needed and greeted the RBA's easing on May 23 with surprise and not a little scepticism.

All that changed when dismal data on April retail sales and May employment showed the economy stumbled badly in the second quarter. Not to be caught out again, the money market rushed to to price in another 50 basis point cut and the dollar extended its downtrend to 3-1/2 months and 5-1/2 cents.

Some still say a cut is not inevitable since leading indicators of the economy are pointing to a pickup and the recent fall in the currency has been a de facto easing in itself, to mention but two of the arguments marshalled by bulls.

This camp was looking for a short covering bounce in the dollar if the bank had not moved by Friday morning but even then recognised the risk would linger until the following board meeting on August 5 and could cap the currency at US$0.7530.
The question of timing was a thorny one for the easing camp as well since there were key domestic data out Wednesday and the Federal Reserve were holding a meeting later the same day.

Many felt the bank would chose to wait and see if, and by how much, retail sales bounced back in May from April's shock 1.7 percent slide A very strong showing might stay its hand while a soft result -- that being anything less than a 1.0 percent rise -- would merely confirm its easing bias.

Furthermore, if it waited until Thursday morning it would also know whether the Fed had stayed put on policy, as the market expects, or taken the plunge by hiking U.S. rates. Were the RBA to cut and the Fed tighten on the same day the impact on the dollar could be grave indeed, with dealers fearing stop loss selling could easily degenerate into a disorderly free fall.

If the Fed did not move, analysts saw Thursday morning as the obvious time for the RBA to act. If it stayed silent, the market would assume an easing was on hold until inflation and wages data later in the month and the dollar could rally.
Even the likely reaction to an easing was difficult to gauge since dealers judged the dollar had already fallen over a cent in anticipation and was very oversold on weekly charts.
The crucial factor may be whether the market sees it as last cut in the cycle, or fears yet another lies in wait if the economy does not show clear signs of improvement.
